newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition sticks to election demands.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition sticks to election demands.

text.p: Pro-democracy demonstrators, their enthusiasm unbowed in a waiting game with the Serbian government, marched through Belgrade on Thursday in a 75th straight day of protests.

The capital was rife with rumours of a cabinet reshuffle and hints that authoritarian President Slobodan Milosevic would offer dialogue with the opposition but protesters said they would not be diverted by compromise solutions.

Opposition leaders promised to keep up street protests until Milosevic's Socialist Party (SPS) conceded defeat in November municipal elections whose results were annulled in 14 major towns and cities, including Belgrade.
"We have been here for 70 days but we shall last 700 days if need be," Zoran Djindjic, a leader of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition, told supporters on Wednesday evening.

Some 15,000 students marched through Belgrade on Thursday without hindrance by weary riot police who appear to have relaxed a ban on protest marches, raising speculation that Milosevic was preparing to offer talks with Zajedno.
A senior Russian diplomat said as much after meeting the reclusive Milosevic on Tuesday.

"They say the president has some new ideas, he will announce them in a day or two...We say we will listen to all of his ideas -- but only after the November 17 election results are recognised," Djindjic said.
The students snarled downtown traffic and many Belgraders came out on their apartment balconies to blow whistles and bang pans in solidarity as they filed noisily by.
Discontent with the government's political aloofness and economic mismanagement spread this week with the outbreak of strikes by school teachers and Belgrade lawyers.

Independent local media said classes had stopped at more than 600 primary and secondary schools in Serbia with teachers demanding payment of overdue salaries and dismissal of the unpopular education minister.

Teachers are among various groups of public employees who have not been regularly paid for some time, reflecting the woes of an economy drained by socialist inefficiency and state coffers looted by corrupt apparatchiks.
A group of 17 independent economists, saying the protests showed the public wanted fundamental change, called this week for sweeping free-market reforms to salvage the economy.

The Belgrade Chamber of Attorneys said it would stage daily protest marches over what it called the "disastrous state" of the Yugoslav federal judiciary and "enormous abuses of political power in influencing court decisions".
Socialist hardliners have used politically subservient courts to invalidate Zajedno election victories in some towns and obstruct the handover of others to the opposition.
Belgrade's electoral commission bucked Socialist pressure and declared this month that the opposition had won the capital vote only to see its verdict quashed by two local courts.

Socialists plan to convene a new city council based on a subsequent round of elections boycotted by Zajedno, but the commission said it would not confirm the results as required by law pending a Supreme Court ruling on a Zajedno appeal.
Diplomats say the election dispute has sunk into a legalistic swamp in the absence of clear, public directions from Milosevic on a way out of the political imbroglio.
He has remained pointedly silent on the opposition's demand for recognition of their election triumphs but has also hesitated to stifle their protests with brute police force.
Most analysts say Milosevic, wary of incurring renewed international sanctions, has allowed the protests to go on for too long to simply crush them with police now.
The demonstrations have evolved into calls for an end to Milosevic's rule and five decades of unbroken power by the Socialists and their communist predecessors.
While the protests have isolated and humiliated Milosevic, they have not extracted significant concessions from him in part because they have not drawn supportive general strikes.
Real unemployment exceeds 50 percent and workers, whether still on the job or not, fear dismissal if they strike and are preoccupied making ends meet for their families.
